questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: When an electrical current stimulates a nerve fibre, the surface of the plasma membrane nearer the cathode becomes:

options.A: More positive, reducing excitability
options.B: More negative relative to the opposite surface, which can reduce the resting potential difference across the membrane on the cathode side and initiate an impulse if it falls enough for sodium permeability to increase
options.D: Permanently depolarised with no possibility of returning to rest

questions.explanation: The membrane surface nearer the cathode becomes more negative. On the side of the nerve nearer the cathode, this additional charge is of opposite polarity to the resting membrane potential, reducing the potential difference (PD) across it — if the PD falls enough for the membrane to become permeable to sodium ions, an impulse is initiated.
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Mechanism of Nerve Stimulation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: High fevers occurring specifically at night, associated with night sweats, may be an early indicator of which condition?

options.A: Simple viral cold
options.B: Pulmonary tuberculosis
options.D: Musculoskeletal chest pain

questions.explanation: High fevers occurring at night with associated night sweats may be the first indicator of pulmonary tuberculosis, and should prompt further investigation.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Other Symptoms
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: On the International Death Certificate, Part II records:

options.A: The direct/immediate cause of death only
options.B: Other significant conditions that contributed to the death but were not directly related to the disease or condition causing it
options.D: Only conditions unrelated to the patient's death in any way

questions.explanation: Part II of the death certificate records other significant associated conditions that contributed to the death but did not directly lead to it (e.g. diabetes as a contributing but non-causal condition), distinct from Part I, which records the direct cause and the underlying/antecedent causes forming the direct chain to death.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Measurement of Mortality — International Death Certificate
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: A stroke patient has nonfluent, slow, hesitant speech with a limited vocabulary, but relatively preserved auditory comprehension. This is classically associated with a lesion of:

options.A: Wernicke's area, in the posterior temporal gyrus
options.B: Broca's area, in the third frontal convolution of the dominant hemisphere
options.D: The cerebellum

questions.explanation: This is classic Broca's (nonfluent, expressive) aphasia — slow, effortful, nonfluent speech with a limited vocabulary but relatively preserved comprehension — caused by a lesion of Broca's area in the dominant (typically left) frontal lobe. Wernicke's (fluent, receptive) aphasia, by contrast, produces fluent but often meaningless speech with impaired comprehension.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Middle Cerebral Artery Syndrome
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: When an apparent outbreak of infection is investigated and 'typing' shows the causal organisms do NOT share identical phenotypic/genotypic characteristics, the event is instead termed a:

options.A: True outbreak
options.B: Pseudo-outbreak
options.D: Case-control study

questions.explanation: Confirmation of a genuine infectious disease outbreak usually requires typing evidence that the causal organisms share identical phenotypic and/or genotypic characteristics. If this is not the case, the apparent cluster is termed a pseudo-outbreak rather than a true outbreak.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Epidemiology of Infection — Outbreaks of Infection
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: Haemozoin (acid haematin, malarial pigment) is distinguished from haemosiderin by which key laboratory feature?

options.A: Haemozoin stains positive with Perl's Prussian blue reaction, while haemosiderin does not
options.B: Haemozoin does NOT stain with Perl's Prussian blue reaction, unlike haemosiderin which does
options.C: Both stain identically with every histochemical stain
options.D: Haemozoin is only found in bone marrow, never other tissue

questions.explanation: Unlike haemosiderin, haemozoin (malarial pigment) does NOT stain with Perl's Prussian blue reaction — likely because it forms a complex with protein that prevents the reaction — despite both being haem-iron-derived pigments.
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Acid Haematin
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: Association areas of the cerebral cortex (in the frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes) are now understood to primarily:

options.A: Simply form a direct wired connection between sensory input and motor output with no further processing
options.B: Process and integrate sensory information relayed from primary sensory areas and the thalamus, supporting complex functions like thought, memory, and language
options.C: Have no known function at all
options.D: Exist only in non-human animals, not in humans

questions.explanation: Early researchers thought association areas simply linked sensory input to motor output directly, but they are now understood to process and integrate information from primary sensory areas and the thalamus, supporting higher psychological functions such as thought, memory, imagery, and language before that processed information may be passed on to motor areas.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Association Cortex, Behavior, and Experience
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: Why can a meniscal injury sometimes present with little or no pain or swelling, making diagnosis more difficult?

options.A: The menisci are avascular and have no nerve supply on their inner two-thirds
options.B: The menisci are the most richly innervated structures in the knee
options.C: Meniscal tears always occur alongside complete ACL rupture, masking symptoms
options.D: Meniscal tissue regenerates immediately after injury

questions.explanation: The menisci are avascular and lack nerve supply on their inner two-thirds, meaning an injury confined to this region can produce little or no pain or swelling — one reason meniscal injury can be difficult to diagnose confidently without a thorough history and examination.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Tests for Meniscus Injury
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: The existence of 'spare receptors' (receptor reserve) explains which observed phenomenon?

options.A: Some full agonists can produce a maximal response while occupying less than 1% of available receptors
options.B: All antagonists eventually become agonists at high enough doses
options.C: Receptor numbers never change regardless of chronic drug exposure
options.D: Enzymes and receptors are functionally identical structures

questions.explanation: When a tissue has a large receptor reserve, a full agonist can produce its maximal biological response by occupying only a small fraction of the total available receptors — occupying more receptors beyond that doesn't increase the effect further, since the response has already plateaued.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: In a child presenting with acute scrotal pain, testicular torsion must be relieved within approximately what time window from symptom onset for a good chance of testicular salvage?

options.A: 6-8 hours
options.B: 48 hours
options.D: There is no time limit

questions.explanation: Testicular torsion must be relieved within 6-8 hours of symptom onset for a good chance of salvaging the testis — this is why any acute scrotum where torsion cannot be confidently excluded requires urgent surgical exploration.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — The Acute Scrotum
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: During fetal development, which period (18-55 days of gestation) is considered the MOST vulnerable to drug-induced structural deformities?

options.A: Fertilization and implantation
options.B: Organogenesis
options.D: The period immediately after birth

questions.explanation: Organogenesis (roughly 18-55 days of gestation) is the most vulnerable period for teratogen-induced structural deformities, since organs are actively forming during this window. Exposure during fertilization/implantation more often causes early pregnancy failure, while exposure during growth and development (56 days onward) tends to cause functional rather than structural abnormalities.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Adverse Drug Effects — Teratogenicity
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) is a clot-dissolving therapy for acute ischemic stroke. Within what time window from symptom onset must it generally be given to be effective and safe?

options.A: 24 hours
options.B: 3 hours
options.D: There is no time limit

questions.explanation: tPA must generally be given within 3 hours of symptom onset to be effective, and cannot be given in hemorrhagic stroke because it may worsen bleeding — this is why rapid recognition of stroke symptoms and emergency imaging (CT) to distinguish ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke are critical ('time is brain').
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Risk Factors and Stroke Prevention
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Clarke's sign and the McConnell test are both special tests associated with which condition?

options.A: Patellofemoral syndrome
options.B: Iliotibial band friction syndrome
options.D: Leg length discrepancy

questions.explanation: Clarke's sign and the McConnell test are both used in the assessment of patellofemoral syndrome (anterior knee pain related to patellar tracking/compression issues).
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Special Tests Commonly Performed on the Knee
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Edman's reagent (phenylisothiocyanate) is used in protein sequencing chiefly because it allows:

options.A: Complete hydrolysis of the protein into free amino acids only
options.B: Selective labelling and removal of the N-terminal amino acid as a PTH-derivative, leaving the rest of the polypeptide intact for repeated cycles
options.C: Cleavage of the protein only at cysteine residues
options.D: Permanent, irreversible denaturation of all peptide bonds

questions.explanation: Unlike Sanger's reagent (which labels and then requires full hydrolysis, destroying the polypeptide), Edman's reagent selectively removes and identifies the N-terminal amino acid as a phenylthiohydantoin (PTH) derivative while leaving the remaining polypeptide intact — allowing the process to be repeated cycle after cycle to read the sequence progressively.
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Determination of Primary Structure
questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.question: 'Physical dependence' on a drug is best defined as:

options.A: Simply enjoying the effects of a drug with no physiological consequence of stopping it
options.B: An altered physiological state (neuroadaptation) requiring the continued presence of the drug to maintain equilibrium, such that stopping it produces a characteristic withdrawal syndrome
options.C: A purely psychological craving with no biological basis whatsoever
options.D: A condition seen only with stimulant drugs like cocaine and amphetamines

questions.explanation: Physical dependence is an altered physiological state produced by repeated drug administration, requiring the drug's continued presence to maintain equilibrium ('neuroadaptation'); stopping the drug produces a characteristic withdrawal syndrome. Drugs like opioids, barbiturates, alcohol, and benzodiazepines produce physical dependence, while stimulants like amphetamines and cocaine produce little or none, despite being highly reinforcing.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Adverse Drug Effects — Drug Dependence
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: The 'plane of least pelvic dimensions' (narrow pelvic plane), a landmark used for pudendal nerve block, corresponds anatomically to approximately the level of:

options.A: The pelvic inlet
options.B: The ischial spines
options.D: The pubic symphysis alone, excluding any posterior landmark

questions.explanation: The plane of least pelvic dimensions extends from the lower border of the symphysis pubis to the tip of the ischial spines, and posteriorly to the 5th sacral vertebra. It is the narrowest plane in the pelvis, roughly corresponds to the origin of levator ani, is where internal rotation of the fetal head occurs, and is the landmark used for pudendal nerve block.
questions.sourceChapter: Fetal Skull and Maternal Pelvis — Outlet
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: In Adult Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), what is emphasised as more diagnostically useful than the radiographic appearance alone?

options.A: The timing of the radiographic changes relative to the insult and onset of symptoms
options.B: The patient's blood type
options.C: The exact colour of the consolidation on the film
options.D: The time of day the X-ray was taken

questions.explanation: In ARDS, it is the TIMING of radiographic changes relative to the inciting insult and the onset of clinical symptoms — rather than the radiological appearance alone (which resembles pulmonary oedema) — that helps suggest the diagnosis, since the chest radiograph is often normal in the initial hours despite clinical distress.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Thoracic Imaging — Adult Respiratory Distress Syndrome
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: After a fracture of both the radius and ulna shafts, why must cross-union (bony union between the two bones) be specifically prevented during healing?

options.A: Cross-union has no functional consequence
options.B: Cross-union would permanently fuse the radius and ulna together, abolishing pronation and supination of the hand
options.C: Cross-union only affects elbow flexion, not the hand
options.D: It increases the risk of scaphoid fracture

questions.explanation: Pronation and supination depend on the radius being able to rotate around a stable ulna. If the two bones heal fused together (cross-union), that rotation becomes impossible, so surgeons take specific care during fixation of combined radius-ulna shaft fractures to prevent it.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Clinical Anatomy
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: A choristoma differs from a true neoplasm in that it is actually:

options.A: An ectopic island of otherwise normal tissue (heterotopia), not a genuine tumour
options.B: A tumour with two distinct malignant cell lines mixed together
options.C: Exactly the same thing as a hamartoma
options.D: Always fatal within the first year of life

questions.explanation: A choristoma is the name given to ectopic islands of completely normal tissue found in an abnormal location — it is heterotopia, not a true tumour, even though the name sounds like one.
questions.sourceChapter: Neoplasia — Special Categories of Tumours
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: Low-dose aspirin helps prevent myocardial infarction and stroke primarily by:

options.A: Inhibiting thromboxane A2 formation, thereby preventing platelet aggregation
options.B: Directly dissolving existing arterial plaques
options.D: Stimulating prostacyclin breakdown

questions.explanation: Aspirin inhibits thromboxane A2 formation, which in turn prevents platelet aggregation — this is the physiological basis for using low-dose aspirin in the prevention of myocardial infarction and stroke.
questions.sourceChapter: Platelets or Thrombocytes — Functions, Important Note on Aspirin
